cultivar: Yunnan large-leaf (Camellia sinensis var. assamica), old seed-grown Jingmai and Mangjing gardens with relatively small leaves for the type
processing: Raw pu-erh: pan-fired, rolled, sun-dried maocha, steamed and pressed into cakes. Jingmai leaf is thinner than Menghai leaf, so good producers use a quick, light kill-green to protect the orchid aroma.
harvest_season: Spring (late March to April) is the reference harvest and the most fragrant; autumn tea is noticeably cheaper and softer.
appearance_dry: Slender, tightly twisted dark-green leaves with small silvery buds, pressed into a neat medium-tight cake.
appearance_liquor: Bright pale gold, very clear, with an aroma that reaches you before the cup does.
appearance_wet: Smallish, even, yellow-green leaves, thinner and more delicate than Bulang or Yiwu material.
taste_profile: High orchid and honeysuckle fragrance, a sharp but short bitterness with some astringency, honey sweetness and a cooling, perfumed finish; lighter-bodied than most Menghai teas.

brewing.notes: Rinse once, briefly. A thin-walled gaiwan shows the aroma best; keep the first three steeps very short, because the astringency arrives before the sweetness if you linger.

vintage_note: Sold by spring harvest year and by village or garden (Jingmai Dazhai, Mangjing, Nuogang, Wengji, the Dapingzhang forest gardens), as cakes and increasingly as loose maocha and dragon balls. It is a tea drunk mostly young (1–5 years) for its fragrance; the mid-aged window of 5–12 years mellows the astringency into honey but softens the florals, and very old Jingmai is rare because the mountain only became a named origin around the mid-2000s. Since the 2023 World Heritage listing the name has become more valuable, so check that 'Jingmai' tea comes from the old forest gardens and not from the newer terraced plantations around them; dry storage suits it.
description:
Jingmai Shan is a forest mountain in Lancang County, Pu'er prefecture, where Dai and Bulang villages have farmed tea under the tree canopy for centuries, and in 2023 its old tea forests were inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage cultural landscape, the first tea landscape to get that status. The tea is instantly recognisable by its scent: an intense orchid and honeysuckle fragrance that Chinese drinkers call 'lan xiang'.

The gardens sit at roughly 1,200–1,600 m and are not plantations but tea trees growing among forest, with moss and the parasitic 'crab claw' plant (pangxiejiao) on the oldest trunks. The leaf is thinner and smaller than typical Menghai leaf. It is made the usual sheng way, pan-fired, rolled and sun-dried, and careful producers keep the firing light because that fragrance is easy to cook away.

In the cup, young Jingmai is bright and perfumed, with a bitterness that is sharp but brief, a distinct astringency on the sides of the tongue and a honeyed, cooling finish. The body is lighter than Bulang or Yiwu, so it is a tea of aroma and aftertaste rather than weight. The way to ruin it is a long first steep: the grip comes out before the sweetness. Flash it early and it stays elegant for ten infusions.

It is sold by spring year and village, and the two famous old forest areas are Jingmai (Dai villages) and Mangjing (Bulang villages). Because the mountain also has large terraced plantations planted in the twentieth century, a 'Jingmai gushu' at a plantation price is usually just plantation tea, which is still fragrant but thinner and harsher. The crab claw plant is sold separately as a tisane and sometimes brewed together with the tea.

If you enjoy aromatic oolongs and find most sheng too heavy, Jingmai is the entry point; drink it within its first five years, when the fragrance is at its peak.
sources_note: UNESCO inscription of the 'Cultural Landscape of Old Tea Forests of the Jingmai Mountain in Pu'er' was in September 2023; the claim that it is the first tea-themed World Heritage site is widely reported.
history:
Jingmai Mountain, in Lancang County, Pu'er prefecture, is farmed by Dai and Bulang villages who grow tea under the forest canopy, and the arrangement is old enough that local accounts speak of many centuries. Its old tea forests are now a UNESCO World Heritage cultural landscape, which has made the name far more valuable.

As a named origin on pu-erh wrappers it is fairly modern. The mountain also has newer terraced plantations, so the label alone says little about which trees are in the cake.
